title: Chapter VIII

context.history: Fitzgerald alternates Nick's account with the testimony of Michaelis, the Greek coffee-shop owner beside Wilson's garage, as at an inquest. Wilson's belief that the billboard eyes are God's draws on the period's loss of traditional faith that writers such as T. S. Eliot (The Waste Land, 1922) described.

significance: Gatsby dies waiting for a call that never comes, still loyal to Daisy; Wilson, misled by Tom, becomes the instrument of the rich couple's carelessness. Nick's compliment is the only judgment he speaks aloud to Gatsby.

segments.script: Fitzgerald alternates Nick's account with the testimony of Michaelis, the Greek coffee-shop owner beside Wilson's garage, as at an inquest. Wilson's belief that the billboard eyes are God's draws on the period's loss of traditional faith that writers such as T. S. Eliot (The Waste Land, 1922) described. Gatsby dies waiting for a call that never comes, still loyal to Daisy; Wilson, misled by Tom, becomes the instrument of the rich couple's carelessness. Nick's compliment is the only judgment he speaks aloud to Gatsby. Characterization: Gatsby tells Nick about Daisy in 1917; he waits in vain for her call. Symbolism: Wilson sees Eckleburg's eyes as God's. Structure: Gatsby is shot in his pool. Watch for the green light: The light at the end of Daisy's dock: Gatsby's dream, distant and unreachable, and finally the "orgiastic future" that recedes before everyone. In this chapter: “stood there for a minute and then turned out the light” (Chapter VIII, paragraph 3).
